segments.voice: Yesterday, the hymn asked Kardama, the mud, to bring the lotus mother home: fortune rising clean from the mud. Today, a new hymn, made of names.
screen: `KARDAMA, BRING HER HOME.` · `FORTUNE RISING CLEAN FROM THE MUD.`

segments.voice: At seven in the morning she's Mom, hunting for a missing shoe. By nine she's Doctor, signing charts. At lunch a friend calls her by a nickname from college. At the temple an old aunty calls her beta, child. Same woman. Every name catches a different side of her, and nobody who loves her would pick just one. Now make that vast. The Lalita Sahasranama is a hymn made almost entirely of names for the goddess, one after another, line after line. Today, how it opens.
screen: `MOM AT SEVEN. DOCTOR BY NINE.` → `EVERY NAME, A DIFFERENT SIDE.` → `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Sahasranama means a thousand names, and Lalita is the goddess they belong to. Tradition places the hymn in the Brahmanda Purana, as a teaching the god Hayagriva gives to the sage Agastya. Some who worship her recite it name by name, at home or in temples. A hymn of names works differently from a story. There's no plot. Each name is a small window, and you look through one, then the next. Over the coming days the path will open a few of those windows, not all of them. So, the first three names, in paraphrase. Sri Mata: the auspicious Mother. Sri Maharajni: the great Queen. Srimat Simhasaneshvari: she who rules from the glorious lion throne. Notice the order. Mother first, before the crown, before the throne, before any of her power is named. Some teachers say that's the key to the whole hymn: whatever she is later, a warrior, a queen, the power behind the universe, she is that as a mother, and the one reciting comes to her as a child. Then the throne and the lion: royal names. And the very first sound is Sri, the word the Sri Sukta days were built on. Here is the teaching under the order. This is Shakta devotion, the worship of God as the Goddess, and its first move is to call the highest power Mother. You don't come to her as a subject with a petition. You come as her child. That's why so many Hindus simply say Ma, at the temple, at the home shrine, under their breath in a hard week. Not a lesser name. The first one.
screen: `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.` · `SRI MATA, THE MOTHER.` · `GREAT QUEEN, ON THE LION THRONE.` · `YOU COME AS HER CHILD.` · then, large: `MOTHER BEFORE QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Try what devotees do with this hymn: say the first three names slowly, Sri Mata, Sri Maharajni, Srimat Simhasaneshvari, with folded hands, or a flower or a pinch of kumkum for each if you have a shrine. Then say only the first one a few more times, and rest there. If you don't pray, say the meanings in English, Mother, great Queen, the one on the lion throne, and notice which one feels closest.
The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn of names for the goddess Lalita, which opens Sri Mata, the Mother, before Queen or throne.
Your line: the goddess is mother before she is queen. Sri Mata comes first. See you tomorrow.

1101.title: Out of the fire
1101.hook: the gods offer everything into a fire, and Lalita rises from it, ready for their work
1101.tomorrow: a noose, a hook, a bow of sugarcane. why is she holding those?
1101.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Lalita Sahasranama before a lamp or a sacred fire, and in Sri Vidya worship the recitation is sometimes joined to fire offerings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama opened with Sri Mata, the Mother, before Queen and throne. Today, two more names, and a fire.

The gods have run out of answers. A demon has the upper hand, and nothing they've tried has worked. So, in the story told around this hymn, they build a great fire and begin a sacrifice. They pour in offerings, and then, when the offerings aren't enough, tradition says they begin to offer themselves. The fire roars higher. And out of the flames a goddess rises: radiant, calm, and already knowing what she's come to do. That is Lalita's arrival. Today, the two names that hold that moment.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE RUN OUT OF ANSWERS.` → `A FIRE, AND A SACRIFICE.` → `OUT OF THE FLAMES, A GODDESS.`

segments.voice: Here are the names, in paraphrase. The fourth: she who was born from the fire-altar of consciousness. The fifth: she who rose up, ready for the work of the gods. Start with the fire. In the story, it's a real sacrifice, an altar with flames. But the name doesn't say a fire of wood. It says a fire of consciousness: chit, awareness itself. So the hymn quietly turns the story inward. Some commentators read the fire-altar as also the heart of the one who sits and recites. Notice where she isn't born. Not from a womb, not from a bargain. From a fire. Then the second name, and it's practical. She rose up ready for the work of the gods. She doesn't arrive to be admired; she arrives with a task. Put the two names side by side and you have the tradition's big word for her: Shakti, power. In Shakta teaching the divine isn't a still light that sits apart while someone else does the work. The goddess is consciousness itself, and she is also its power to move, to make, to help. Awareness and action, one goddess, risen from one fire. That's why a devotee can sit in silence with her at dawn, then ask her for strength before a hard day, and know it's the same Mother.

segments.voice: If you have a lamp or a candle, light it, the way many Hindus light a diya before reciting; if not, picture one. Near the end, let one plain question rise out of the stillness, what work is mine today, without forcing an answer. If you pray, offer the question to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let it sit with you.

segments.voice: A rope. A hook for steering an elephant. A bow cut from sugarcane. Arrows tipped with flowers. That's what the goddess Lalita holds in her four hands, in paintings and temple images. An odd inventory: a noose and a goad sound like tools for catching and driving animals, and a sugarcane bow sounds like something out of a children's story. But the Lalita Sahasranama doesn't leave the objects as objects. A short run of names, early in the hymn, says what each one really is.
screen: `A ROPE, A HOOK, A BOW, ARROWS.` → `AN ODD INVENTORY.` → `FOUR NAMES FOR FOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: After the names of her rising from a fire of consciousness, the hymn describes her form, and four names in a row say what she carries. In paraphrase: she holds the noose that is desire. The Sanskrit there is raga: passion, attachment, the pull toward what we want. She shines with the goad that is anger, the hooked stick that keeps an elephant moving or turns it aside. Her bow of sugarcane is the mind. And her arrows are the five subtle elements, the tanmatras, the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, what the senses meet. Desire, anger, the mind, the senses. The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on things breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger. These are the hard parts of an inner life, and in this hymn they aren't thrown away or trampled. They're in the goddess's hands. Readers take that more than one way. Some say she holds them, so they have no hold on her. Others hear something gentler: even a person's desire and anger are within her reach. And notice the sweetness: the bow is sugarcane, the arrows are flowers, as in the old stories Kama, the god of love, carries; the path will come back to him tomorrow. Here's the teaching, and you can see it on any shrine: in a Hindu image, what the god holds is a lesson. Lalita's hands say the hard parts of a person aren't outside the divine. They're held, and steered, the way a goad steers an elephant instead of killing it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want you're carrying today and notice it the way you'd notice a rope in someone's hand: there, held; then one irritation, then the busy mind, then one sound or touch, each seen the same way. Nothing to fix. If you pray, you can offer each to the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let them rest in open hands.
The Lalita Sahasranama. The hymn of names for the goddess Lalita, and today four of them: the noose, the goad, the bow and the arrows.

1103.title: Love brought back from ash
1103.hook: Lalita wins her war, then brings Kama, love, back from the ash
1103.carry: kama, love, is one of life's four aims

1103.howItsDone: The story of Lalita's war with Bhanda is told in the Lalitopakhyana of the Brahmanda Purana, and devotees who recite the Lalita Sahasranama pass through the battle in a run of its names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama put four things in the goddess's hands: the noose that is desire, the goad that is anger, the bow that is the mind.

What happens to love after it's been burned to ash? In the old stories, Kama, the god of love, once aimed his flower arrows at Shiva in meditation. Shiva opened his third eye, and Kama was burned to nothing. The story told alongside the Lalita Sahasranama picks up from there. Tradition says something grew out of those ashes: a demon named Bhanda, who brought misery to the worlds until the gods offered themselves into a sacrificial fire and the goddess Lalita rose from it. Then comes a war, and the hymn, mostly names, tells the war in names too.
screen: `KAMA BURNED TO ASH.` → `A DEMON FROM THE ASHES.` → `A WAR TOLD IN NAMES.`

segments.voice: Read a stretch slowly and the story moves under the names like a river under ice. In paraphrase: she delights in the courage of her powers as they cut down Bhanda's army. She delights in the young goddess Bala, who strikes down Bhanda's sons. She glances at the face of Kameshvara, her consort, and from that glance Ganesha is formed. She rejoices when Ganesha shatters the device the demons built to block her army. Then the end: with Kameshvara's own weapon she burns Bhanda, and his city with him, and the gods praise her glory. A fine place to finish. But the hymn adds one more name, and it's the surprise. She is the life-giving herb for Kama, who was burned by the fire of Shiva's eye. After the battle, she brings love back. Hold that next to yesterday: Lalita carries the same sugarcane bow and flower arrows Kama carried. The hymn doesn't treat desire as an enemy to destroy forever. What grew wrong out of the ash is defeated, and the one who was burned is restored. Many teachers read Bhanda as desire gone wrong. It fits something Hinduism says plainly. The tradition names four aims of a human life: dharma, doing what's right; artha, a livelihood; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom. Kama is on the list. Wanting itself isn't the enemy. The hymn won't let a war be the last word about her. Healing is.

1104.title: The one who hides
1104.hook: the hymn's five acts of the goddess, and two of them are hiding and grace
1104.carry: hiding is hers, and so is grace
1104.tomorrow: a jeweled city, and a second address inside the body
1104.howItsDone: In the Shakta reading of the Lalita Sahasranama, the goddess performs the five cosmic acts through the forms of Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Ishvara and Sadashiva; in Shaiva traditions the same five acts are attributed to Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama told a war in names, and ended it with Kama, love, brought back from ash.

A baby on a kitchen floor, and a grown-up behind a dish towel. The towel goes up, the face is gone, and the baby goes still, a little worried. The towel comes down, there's the face again, and the baby shrieks with laughter. Peekaboo only works because of the hiding: without the moment of not-seeing, there's nothing to find. Today the Lalita Sahasranama does something like it on a cosmic scale. In a short run of names, it lists what the goddess does with the whole universe. Some of it is expected. Two of the acts are not.
screen: `A FACE BEHIND A DISH TOWEL.` → `NO HIDING, NOTHING TO FIND.` → `WHAT SHE DOES WITH THE UNIVERSE.`

segments.voice: Here is the run, in paraphrase. She is the maker, in the form of Brahma. The protector, in the form of Govinda, a name of Vishnu. The one who draws everything back in, in the form of Rudra. The one who conceals, as Ishvara, the Lord. She is Sadashiva, the giver of grace. And a name gathers them up: she is devoted to the five acts. Making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing and grace. Two things stand out. First, the great gods appear as forms the goddess takes. In Shaiva traditions the same five acts belong to Shiva; in this hymn to the goddess they are hers, and the gods are her ways of doing them. Second, after withdrawal comes concealment. The Sanskrit is tirodhana: hiding, veiling. Some teachers who use this list say it's the act that makes the world seem to be only itself, so the deeper reality behind it is out of sight. Then the last act: anugraha, grace, favor, the turning toward someone. The towel coming down. Some readers take the order seriously: concealing comes before grace, the way hiding comes before finding. Either way, here's the teaching. When God feels far away, this tradition doesn't read it as God gone. Hiding is one of her own acts, and grace is on the same list. Devotees in a dry season of prayer lean on that: the distance is hers too, and so is the turning back. The one who hides is the one who reveals.
screen: `MAKING, KEEPING, WITHDRAWING.` · `THE GODS AS HER FORMS.` · `CONCEALING: TIRODHANA.` · `GRACE: ANUGRAHA.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO HIDES IS THE ONE WHO REVEALS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes for a few breaths and let the room be concealed: the chair, the walls, the light are all still there, you just can't see them. Then slowly open your eyes and let the room come back, as if it were being handed to you; close them and rest, open them and receive, each opening unhurried. If you pray, you can greet the goddess in what returns, in your own words; if you don't, just notice what it's like to be given the room again.
The Lalita Sahasranama. Today, its five acts of the goddess: making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing, and grace.
Your line: hiding is hers, and so is grace. The one who hides is the one who reveals. Until tomorrow.

1105.howItsDone: In Shakta Tantra and the Sri Vidya tradition, the kundalini names of the Lalita Sahasranama are read as a map of inner practice taught by a guru; other devotees simply recite them as praise of the goddess within.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama named the goddess's five acts: making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing and grace.

Same goddess, two addresses. Early in the Lalita Sahasranama she lives somewhere grand. The names place her in the middle of an ocean of nectar, in a forest of kadamba trees, in a house of wish-granting gems, seated on a throne. A palace you'd need a map to find. Then, further on, the hymn turns and gives her a second address, and this one isn't far away at all. It's a human body, starting at the base of the spine.
screen: `AN OCEAN OF NECTAR, A HOUSE OF GEMS.` → `THEN A SECOND ADDRESS.` → `INSIDE A HUMAN BODY.`

segments.voice: Here is the run, in paraphrase, and it moves like a climb. Her one dwelling is the muladhara, the root center at the base of the spine. She pierces the knot of Brahma. She rises within the manipura, the center at the navel. She pierces the knot of Vishnu. She stands within the ajna, the center between the brows. She pierces the knot of Rudra. She rises onto the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, and from there she pours down streams of nectar. A few names on, the hymn calls her bright as a streak of lightning, dwelling above the six centers, and names her outright: Kundalini, the coiled one, fine as the thread inside a lotus stalk. So the queen of the jeweled city is also a power curled at the root of a human body, rising, untying knots and raining nectar back down. In Shakta Tantra and in the Sri Vidya tradition these names are read as a map for inner practice, and those practices are taught by a teacher, in person, with care. This path doesn't teach them. Others hear the names devotionally: the goddess isn't only out there. And here's the teaching under both, one Tantra says loudest: the body isn't a cage the spirit puts up with. It's where the goddess lives. Kundalini isn't a gym word; it's her name. So the way you sleep, eat and sit can count as care for a home of the divine.
screen: `FROM THE ROOT OF THE SPINE.` · `THROUGH THREE KNOTS.` · `TO THE LOTUS AT THE CROWN.` · `KUNDALINI, THE COILED ONE.` · then, large: `THE BODY IS HER HOME TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit tall without strain and feel where you meet the chair or the floor, the base of the spine, solid and supported; then let attention move slowly to the belly rising and falling, to the space between the brows, to the crown of the head. No pushing, no picturing energy, just noticing, place by place, the way you'd walk up a staircase in your own house. If you pray, you can greet the goddess at each step; if you don't, let the climb be quiet.
The Lalita Sahasranama. Today, the names that give the goddess a second home: rising from the root of the spine to the lotus at the crown.
Your line: the body is the goddess's home too. Kundalini is her name. Same time tomorrow.

1106.title: Without form
1106.hook: names that say devotion wins her, then names that say she is without form
1106.carry: saguna and nirguna: near, and beyond form
1106.tomorrow: who wrote the thousand names, and who may say them?
1106.howItsDone: Devotees reciting the Lalita Sahasranama pass from names that praise her form and her closeness to devotees into names that call her formless and beyond qualities, and different Hindu schools explain the relation of saguna and nirguna in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama gave the goddess a second address: rising from the root of the spine to the lotus at the crown. Today closes a week.

Sanskrit has a small prefix, nir, that works a lot like the English word without. Put it in front of a word and the word turns inside out. In the Lalita Sahasranama there's a stretch where name after name begins that way: without support, without stain, without form. What makes the run startling is what comes just before it. A few names earlier, the hymn has been saying the warmest things about her: how close she is, how easily she's reached.
screen: `NIR: A LOT LIKE WITHOUT.` → `NAME AFTER NAME.` → `NEARNESS, AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: First, the nearness. In paraphrase: she is fond of devotion, reached through devotion, won over by devotion, and she is the one who takes fear away. A goddess you could talk to across a kitchen table. Then, a little further on, the other run. Without support, needing nothing to stand on. Stainless. Untouched by anything. Pure. Eternal. Without form. Without agitation. Without qualities, nirguna. Without parts. Peaceful. Without desire. The hymn that painted her face, her four hands, her throne, now says she has no form at all. Hindu thinkers have names for these two ways of speaking. Saguna: with qualities, the goddess you can see, praise and love. Nirguna: beyond qualities, the reality no picture can hold. Teachers in different schools weigh the two differently. Some say the formless is the deeper truth and the forms are a kindness to us. Others say the form is no lesser thing, that she is fully present in it. The hymn keeps both in the same breath. And notice one name in the run: without desire. Four days ago, desire was the noose in her hand. The hymn is happy to say both. That fits the week: the mother and the fire, the inner life in her hands, a war that ended in love restored, five acts, a home in the body. Now no address can hold her. It's also why a Hindu can bow to a small picture on a shelf and, in the same breath, say God has no form. Not a contradiction. Two true ways of speaking, and the hymn uses both.
screen: `WON OVER BY DEVOTION.` · `WITHOUT FORM, WITHOUT QUALITIES.` · `SAGUNA AND NIRGUNA.` · `BOTH IN THE SAME BREATH.` · then, large: `NO ADDRESS CAN HOLD HER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a face, an image or a word that feels close to you, something you could speak to, and let it be near; then gently let the picture go and stay with what's left, the breath, the quiet, the room. Let the picture come back if it wants to, and move between the two without choosing. If you pray, you can rest with the goddess, or with God, in either way; if you don't, simply notice the difference.
The Lalita Sahasranama. Today, names of nearness, won over by devotion, and names of without: without form, without qualities, without parts.
Your line: saguna and nirguna, near, and beyond form, in the same breath. A week walked.
